# Essential nucleus-apical pole linkage maintains division ﬁdelity during Plasmodium progeny formation

Buyuan He 1,6, Ilzat Ali 2,3,6, Lilian P Dorner 1, Monami Roy Chowdhury1, Yvonne Sokolowski-Adams1, Evgeniya Abadzhieva1, Arne Reich1, Marilena Wittmaack 1, Julia M Sattler 1,4, Friedrich Frischknecht 1,4 & Jeffrey D Dvorin 3,5

# Abstract

Plasmodium parasites, the causative agents of malaria, undergo complex replication within vertebrate and insect hosts, presenting unique opportunities for therapeutic intervention. A key challenge during these replication events, i.e., schizogony in vertebrate red blood cells and sporogony in oocysts within mosquitos, is ensuring the faithful partitioning of nuclei and organelles into the numerous daughter cells that form at once from a single parental cell. While nuclear microtubule-organizing centers, or centriolar plaques (CPs), have been hypothesized to play a central role in this process, the molecular mediators linking CPs and organelles remain incompletely deﬁned. Here, we characterize the roles of two striated ﬁber assemblin (SFA) homologs, SFA1 and SFA2, in replication of Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium berghei across two hosts. We show that these SFAs form a physical bridge between the CP and the nascent apical poles of daughter cells, facilitating high- ﬁdelity progeny formation during schizogony and sporogony. Loss of SFA function disrupts merozoite and sporozoite formation, with profound consequences for transmission. These ﬁndings identify striated ﬁber assemblins as essential organizers of parasite morphogenesis and potential targets for anti-malarial therapies.

## Introduction

Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes and caused by the eukaryotic parasites of the genus Plasmodium, which belongs to the phylum Apicomplexa that also includes other disease-causing parasites such as Toxoplasma and Cryptosporidium. Plasmodium parasites infect a

range of species-speciﬁc vertebrate hosts. Plasmodium falciparum is the deadliest species of human malaria parasites, while Plasmodium berghei infects rodents. Decades of malaria research and public health efforts have led to a substantial decrease in the global burden of the illness as well as improvements in treatment options. However, the emergence of P. falciparum resistance to all available antimalarials and insecticide resistance in mosquitoes have slowed progress toward eradication, signifying a need for the discovery of novel targets for a new generation of antimalarial therapeutics and preventives (Alonso and Noor, 2017; Greenwood et al, 2008; World Health Organization, 2024). The parasite life cycle is complex, encompassing replicative stages inside the intermediate vertebrate host and the deﬁnitive insect host (e.g., Anopheles mosquitoes for P. falciparum and P. berghei). These stages occur in drastically different environments, imposing challenges on the parasite to maintain ﬁdelity in its cellular functions while undergoing morphological changes to adapt to external conditions. Due to these selective pressures, the parasite has evolved essential cellular processes divergent from their host cells that serve as attractive targets for next-generation therapy development. Therefore, improving our understanding of fundamental Plasmodium biology across the various life cycle stages can help address current challenges in malaria eradication. The parasite’s unique modes of replication inside the different hosts represent such divergent processes—the asexual blood stage in the vertebrate host and oocyst development in mosquitoes—both generating many morphologically distinct, haploid daughter cells from a single parent cell (Cowman et al, 2016; Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). Thus, studying the mediators of replication across these distinct hosts provides a holistic view of how the parasite survives and proliferates. Schizogony is the mode of asexual replication inside the vertebrate red blood cells (RBCs) during which daughter cells known as merozoites form inside a single parent cell. To do this, the parasite replicates its DNA and undergoes karyokinesis multiple times without cytokinesis, followed by a single semisynchronous cytokinetic event known as segmentation to generate dozens of merozoites at once (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gerald et al, 2011; Gubbels et al, 2020; Rudlaff et al, 2020). Plasmodium oocyst development at the mosquito midgut wall forms transmissible, haploid daughter cells, or sporozoites, via an analogous asexual replication process known as sporogony (Gubbels et al, 2020; Sinden and Strong, 1978). The parent cell, called an oocyst, completes multiple rounds of endopolygeny-like events, i.e., DNA replication without karyokinesis, while partitioning into putatively distinct islands of cytoplasm known as “sporoblasts.” As individual nuclei are partitioned off, a massive cytokinetic event forms thousands of sporozoites (Araki et al, 2020). These sporozoites subsequently move to the mosquito salivary glands for transmission to a new vertebrate host. Central to Plasmodium’s ability to form many daughter cells in a complex, single round of cytokinesis is the maintenance of cell division ﬁdelity. Successful production of invasive daughter cells requires the inheritance of one nucleus per daughter cell, in addition to a complete set of organelles, including a mitochondrion, an apicoplast, an endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, and the components of the apical complex (Elaagip et al, 2022; Rudlaff et al, 2020; Struck et al, 2005; van Dooren et al, 2005; Verhoef et al, 2021). Interactions or close associations between the different compartments have been shown to occur in Plasmodium and related parasites and might be important for cellularization (Guttery et al, 2020; Oliveira Souza et al, 2022; Vaishnava and Striepen, 2006; Verhoef et al, 2024). In schizonts, the ﬁnal round of karyokinesis and organelle segregation coincides with the cytokinetic event in which the membrane-associated cytoskeletal components of each forming merozoite, the inner membrane complex (IMC) and basal complex, envelop one complete set of organelles (Rudlaff et al, 2020). During oocyst development, massive cytokinesis occurs by a cytoskeleton-assisted budding-like process, with the nucleus and each set of other organelles entering the budding membranes to form sporozoites (Araki et al, 2020). This high-ﬁdelity cellular division in the setting of a complex parent cell with multiple nuclei and multiple copies of each organelle suggests a strict coordination between nuclear division, organellar replication and inheritance, and daughter cell formation. However, the molecular mediators of this coordination are incompletely understood in Plasmodium, representing a major knowledge gap. A physical connection between the nucleus and the budding daughter cell has been established in Toxoplasma gondii. This parasite replicates asexually in the host cell via endodyogeny, a process during which a single parent cell divides into two complete daughter cells. During budding, a ﬁber composed of striated ﬁber assemblin (SFA) homologs links the nuclear envelope-associated microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), or centrosome, and the apical end of dividing daughter cells (Francia et al, 2012). SFA proteins were ﬁrst identiﬁed in the green algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Goodenough and Weiss, 1978; Lechtreck et al, 2002; Lechtreck, 2003; Ringo, 1967; Weber et al, 1993). They are the main components of the root microtubule-associated striated ﬁbers of algal ﬂagella. Interestingly, the asexual forms of Plasmodium and Toxoplasma lack a ﬂagellum, but, in the case of T. gondii, an SFA ﬁber still forms. This ﬁber emerges from the centrosome and terminates inside the apical conoid structure of the forming daughter cell (Engelberg et al, 2025; Francia et al, 2012). Parasites lacking TgSFAs fail to initiate budding, resulting in multinucleated parent cells without discernable daughter cell structures. This observation underscores the importance of SFAs in coordinating cell division. T. gondii and Plasmodium diverged ~540–800 million years ago and have evolved distinct features (Douzery et al, 2004).

Hence, studying the SFAs in Plasmodium across both its bloodstage and mosquito-stage development can illuminate foundational similarities and reveal key variations in how the parasite orchestrates division in different cellular environments. Plasmodium schizogony is also coordinated by the MTOC of each nucleus through spindle dynamics that drive closed mitosis (Francia and Striepen, 2014). The dividing nucleus is closely associated with the forming apical ends of daughter merozoites (Liffner et al, 2023). As the nucleus duplicates and divides, the associated forming apical end also divides. The MTOC is part of the centriolar plaque (CP), a multiprotein complex that includes both nuclear and cytoplasmic components (Moore and Sinden, 1974; Tomasina et al, 2021). The nuclear portion of the CP, or inner-CP, initiates the intranuclear microtubules (Arnot et al, 2011; Bertiaux et al, 2021; Liffner et al, 2023; Simon et al, 2021). It consists of centromeric and kinetochore proteins that coordinate karyokinesis, such as nuclear division cycle 80 protein, PfNuf2, and PfCENH3 (Hoeijmakers et al, 2012; Li et al, 2024a; Volz et al, 2010), in addition to a putative spindle pole body protein that likely bridges the nuclear and cytoplasmic portions of the CP (Machado et al, 2023). A few components of the cytoplasmic portion, or outer-CP, have also been reported, including the centrins (Mahajan et al, 2008; Simon et al, 2021; Voß et al, 2023), an Aurora-related kinase (Reininger et al, 2011), and an Sﬁ1-like protein (Wenz et al, 2023). They appear to contribute to intranuclear microtubule dynamics during schizogony; however, the full function of the outer- CP, including its putative connection to the forming apical pole, is yet to be elucidated. The role of the CP during oocyst development inside the mosquito host is also poorly understood. A rootlet ﬁber connecting the CP with the apical end of budding sporozoites had been visualized by electron microscopy since the 1970s (Schrevel et al, 2008; Sinden and Strong, 1978), but its composition remained unknown. Here, we characterize the two SFA orthologs, PfSFA1/PbSFA1 and PfSFA2/PbSFA2, in P. falciparum during schizogony and P. berghei during sexual stage and oocyst development. Using microscopy, genetics, and biochemical techniques, we establish the critical function of PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 to connect the CP of each nucleus with a nascent apical end inside a schizont, ensuring that the ﬁdelity of merozoite formation is maintained. Furthermore, we identify two additional proteins that interact with PfSFA2, PF3D7_0703600 and PF3D7_1339700, that may also contribute to the apical-nuclear connection. In P. berghei, we ﬁnd that the SFAs make up the rootlet ﬁber during sporozoite formation within oocysts in the mosquito host. Loss of either PbSFA1 or PbSFA2 leads to profound defects during sporozoite budding and a complete lack of salivary gland sporozoites, establishing an essential role for these proteins in the mosquito host and for transmission. These ﬁndings establish SFAs as the critical bridge between the CP and the forming apical pole across two distinct Plasmodium replicative stages and hosts.

## Results

PfSFA2 and likely PfSFA1 connect the centriolar plaque and the forming daughter cell during asexual replication in human RBCs

We identiﬁed two SFA homologs, SFA1 (PF3D7_0803200/ PfSFA1 or PBANKA_1227000/PbSFA1) and SFA2 (PF3D7_1432900/ PfSFA2 or PBANKA_1012000/PbSFA2) in P. falciparum and P. berghei (Fig. 1A; Appendix Fig. S1A). Plasmodium SFA2 is similar in size to SFA proteins in other species, consisting of a short N-terminal head domain and a rod domain that has the characteristic repeat regions of the SFA family predicted to form an α-helical structure by AlphaFold (Jumper et al, 2021; Lechtreck, 2003; Varadi et al, 2023). PfSFA2 and PbSFA2 are largely similar in their amino acid sequence, sharing 66% amino acid identity (Appendix Fig. S1B). Plasmodium SFA1 proteins also contain an α-helical rod domain of similar size to SFA2, but are unique in that they are ~2.5 times the size of a canonical SFA due to a large unstructured head domain. While the C-terminal rod domain regions of PfSFA1 and PbSFA1 are highly conserved, the low conservation in the head domain leads to an overall identity of ~48% (Appendix Fig. S1B). PfSFA1 shares a 30% amino acid identity with TgSFA1 and 40% with TgSFA3, while PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 only share a 25% identity with each other (Appendix Fig. S1B). Similarly, PfSFA2 and TgSFA2 share a slightly higher amino acid identity than PfSFA2 does with PfSFA1. These ﬁndings suggest that Plasmodium SFA1 is more closely related to TgSFA1 and TgSFA3 than to Plasmodium SFA2 and TgSFA2, and that the common ancestor of SFA1 and SFA2 predates the divergence of these species. Our ﬁndings were further corroborated in a recent comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of SFA paralogs (Heiss et al, 2025). To determine the localization of the SFAs in Plasmodium asexual blood stage, we endogenously labeled PfSFA1 or PfSFA2 with a high-avidity spaghetti monster-V5 (smV5) epitope tag (Viswanathan et al, 2015) and visualized them by immunoﬂuorescence assay (IFA) using Airyscan super-resolution microscopy (Figs. 1B and EV1A). The multicopy number of epitopes within the smV5 tag allowed for higher signal and better signal-to-noise ratio compared to lower copy-number epitopes (such as 2xV5), which produced a dimmer ﬂuorescence signal, making it too difﬁcult to robustly pinpoint localization. In schizonts, both PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 localized to a punctate structure near the outer-centriolar plaque (CP), identiﬁed with antibodies against centrins (Liffner et al, 2023; Mahajan et al, 2008). The PfSFA2 signal was observed as soon as the centrin signal appeared at each nucleus, duplicated along with centrin, and appeared the brightest when the inner membrane complex (IMC, anti-PfGAP45 (Jones et al, 2006)) began to expand, signaling the onset of segmentation (Fig. EV1A). Then, it disappeared by the end of segmentation. To decipher more precisely the localization of PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 in schizonts, we performed ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) on three distinct schizogony stages (Fig. 1C). A ﬂuorescent dye conjugated to NHS ester (NHS ester for short) that nonspeciﬁcally stains protein-dense structures allows for visualization of mitotic spindles, CPs, and forming apical ends throughout schizogony (Bertiaux et al, 2021; Liffner et al, 2023). In early schizonts, the duplicated outer-CPs, observed by centrin staining, localized above the intranuclear mitotic spindles and below the protein-dense regions where structural components of daughter cells are forming apical to the nucleus (Fig. 1C, top panel). PfSFA2 localized between each centrin and the forming apical end consistently during asynchronous nuclear divisions. Next, in midschizonts, when the parasite began the ﬁnal round of mitosis, the apical poles duplicated one last time and separated (Fig. 1C, middle

panel). The ﬁrst rhoptry anlage of a pair, the dense globular organelles that house parasite invasion proteins, forms beneath the nascent apical polar ring (APR) (Anaguano et al, 2024; Cowman and Crabb, 2006). At this stage, PfSFA2 continued to bridge the outer-CP and the forming apical region of the daughter cells. Finally, during segmentation, when the basal complex (BC) ring became visible, an elongated PfSFA2 structure was observed between the outer-CP and the fully formed APR, although the PfSFA2-containing structure was not clearly visible by NHS ester alone (Fig. 1C, bottom panel). With U-ExM, PfSFA1-smV5 signal also localized between the outer-CP and the apical pole (Fig. EV1B). However, the localization appeared less robust compared to PfSFA2-smV5. This is likely due to the modiﬁcation of the PfSFA1 C-terminus with a large epitope tag like smV5 interfering with its function. The parasites seemed to fare better with a smaller epitope like 2xMyc (Fig. 2; Appendix Fig. S2A); however, we were unable to visualize the SFAs clearly with this tag. Nonetheless, the presence of a signal between the outer-CP and the apical pole suggests a similar localization pattern between PfSFA1 and PfSFA2, and the difﬁculty in modifying the PfSFA1 C-terminus implies the importance of this protein region in its function.

PfSFA1 and PfSFA2 are important for blood-stage replication and likely belong to a single structure

TgSFA2 and TgSFA3 are essential for endodyogeny (Francia et al, 2012). To test the importance of PfSFAs in blood-stage schizogony, we generated ﬂoxed parasite strains with the endogenous PfSFA1 or PfSFA2 ﬂanked by loxP sequences in a parental parasite that expressed a rapamycin-dimerizable split Cre (DiCre) recombinase (Collins et al, 2013a; Knuepfer et al, 2017; Tiburcio et al, 2019). Given the initial difﬁculty producing the PfSFA1 inducible knockout (iKO) strain, we attempted the modiﬁcation in multiple DiCre-expressing parental strains. Ultimately, the modiﬁcation was successfully achieved in 3D7(pfs47)DiCre strain (Knuepfer et al, 2017), generating the PfSFA1loxP iKO strain. The PfSFA2 inducible knockout parasite (PfSFA2loxP iKO) was generated in the NF54(pfs47) DiCre(CG6)attB strain (Fierro et al, 2023) (Appendix Fig. S2B,C). Both transgenic strains were conﬁrmed for genomic integration by PCR (Appendix Fig. S2D). Upon rapamycin treatment to KO either PfSFA1 or PfSFA2, there was a marked growth defect compared to parasites treated with the negative control (DMSO) (Fig. 2A; Appendix Fig. S2A). To quantify the defect, we used the ratio of the parasite multiplication rates (PMR), deﬁned as the PMR of the KO parasite divided by the PMR of the DMSO control. A higher PMR ratio corresponds to a more ﬁt parasite with a less severe growth defect. We observed a PMR ratio of 56 ± 1% for PfSFA1 iKO parasites and a ratio of 65 ± 4% for PfSFA2-iKO parasites, suggesting a comparable defect between the two lines. We do not attribute this partial growth defect to an incomplete KO since a complete rapamycin-induced excision of the modiﬁed locus was observed for each strain by PCR (Appendix Fig. S2D). Moreover, an absence of PfSFA2-smV5 signal after KO was conﬁrmed by IFA for the PfSFA2loxP iKO strain (Appendix Fig. S2E). Instead, this incomplete defect could be due to a partial rescue by other proteins. PfSFA2 is important for maintaining the ﬁdelity of bloodstage replication

At the end of segmentation, fully formed daughter merozoites were visible by U-ExM, wherein each merozoite was bound by a plasma membrane, containing an APR at its apical end, and a BC at the basal end, all visible by the NHS ester-conjugated dye (Fig. 3A,B; Movie EV1) (Liffner et al, 2023; Morano et al, 2023). In a normal merozoite, a pair of equally sized dense rhoptries were observed protruding from the APR, and 1–3 subpellicular microtubules (SPMTs, yellow) ran along the spine of the merozoite from the APR toward the basal end. Each merozoite also inherited a single mitochondrion (stained by MitoTracker, magenta). Lastly, each daughter merozoite contains exactly one nucleus (blue) necessary for the continuation of the life cycle. To characterize the function of PfSFAs during asexual replication, we arrested parasites at the end of segmentation with a small molecular inhibitor of Protein Kinase G, either Compound-1 (Collins et al, 2013b) or ML10 (Baker et al, 2017), in PfSFA2-present (DMSO) and PfSFA2-absent (Rapa) conditions to visualize morphological defects in merozoite formation. In PfSFA2-absent schizonts, multiple nuclei are found in the residual body, a membrane-bound compartment containing leftover schizont materials after segmentation (Liffner et al, 2023; Rudlaff et al, 2020), whereas all nuclei are packaged into merozoites in a 1:1 ratio in control parasites (Fig. 3A; Movies EV1 and 2). Concurrently, we observed merozoites surrounded by plasma membrane without nuclei in PfSFA2-absent schizonts, suggesting a disruption in the linkage between the nuclei and the forming merozoites (Fig. 3B). We quantiﬁed the number of nucleated (#Nuc = 1) and anucleate (#Nuc = 0) merozoites per schizont in both conditions across three biologically independent experiments and found that nearly all merozoites contained a single nucleus when PfSFA2 was present whereas on average 32 ± 1% of the merozoites lacked a nucleus upon PfSFA2 KO (Fig. 3C).

In addition to the defect in nuclear inheritance, we also observed that the number of rhoptries per APR was highly variable in PfSFA2-absent parasites (Fig. 3B,C). On average, 29 ± 2% of the APRs were associated with more than two rhoptries, while 7 ± 1% of the APRs only had a single rhoptry. Moreover, the sizes of the rhoptries associated with the same APR could vary; some APRs contained rhoptries of relatively similar size, while others were associated with rhoptries of drastically different sizes. Occasionally, we observed detached rhoptries inside merozoites or the residual body, and merozoites with two APRs (Fig. EV2B). Notably, the rhoptry abnormalities were observed in both nucleated and anucleate merozoites, although anucleate merozoites tended to display more pronounced abnormalities in rhoptry size and number. These ﬁndings suggest that PfSFAs are also important for maintaining ﬁdelity of rhoptry pair formation. However, it is unclear whether this is a direct function of the SFAs or a function of other structures proximal to the SFAs, such as the CP. Another notable defect upon PfSFA2 KO was a higher variance in SPMT count per APR. In control parasites, APRs were associated with a single SPMT in 9 ± 2% of APRs. However, when PfSFA2 was absent, 32 ± 2% of APRs are associated with a single SPMT, and 4 ± 1% of APRs had no discernable SPMT signal (Fig. EV2D). We also performed all prior analyses with the double iKO strain and found a similar pattern of morphological defects, with these parasites having a slightly higher variance in phenotype compared to the single iKO parasites, marked by a higher spread of the data points (Fig. EV2C,D). Qualitative analysis of Compound-1-stalled PfSFA1-KO schizonts also revealed similar phenotypes as PfSFA2- KO schizonts, including congregation of nuclei and abnormally formed rhoptries inside residual bodies and anucleate merozoite formation (Fig. EV2A). It is worth noting that the DMSO-treated PfSFA1 iKO and double iKO parasites also exhibited morphological defects to a small degree (Fig. EV2), further demonstrating the hypomorphic nature of these strains, likely caused by epitopetagging at PfSFA1 C-terminus. Nonetheless, the similarity in morphological defects observed between PfSFA2 single iKO and PfSFA1/PfSFA2 double iKO parasites quantitatively and between PfSFA1 single iKO and the other iKO parasites qualitatively further demonstrates that the absence of a single SFA homolog is sufﬁcient to disrupt ﬁber function. During schizogony, vital organelles like the mitochondrion and the apicoplast also expand, divide, and partition into individual merozoites (Rudlaff et al, 2020; Verhoef et al, 2024). Given the centrosome-centered hypothesis of apicomplexan parasite cell division (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020), the presence of anucleate merozoites in PfSFA2 KO parasites presented an opportunity to interrogate the importance of the nucleus (and the CP) for the inheritance of these organelles. We found that 86% of all anucleate merozoites still contained a mitochondrion (Fig. 3B). We also observed apicoplast presence in anucleate merozoites by IFA (Fig. 3D). These ﬁndings show that nuclear inheritance is not required for the successful inheritance of mitochondrion and apicoplast into merozoites, suggesting that the partitioning and/or maintenance of these organelles likely require other factors. Overall, we show that SFAs are important for maintaining the connection between each nucleus and the forming apical pole during blood-stage schizogony. PbSFA1 and PbSFA2 form long ﬁbers connecting the centriolar plaque and the apical polar ring during oocyst development

Next, we aimed at investigating the role of SFAs during oocyst development and sporozoite formation. To examine if the SFAs are part of the rootlet ﬁber during sporozoite formation (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019), we used Plasmodium berghei to characterize PbSFA1 and PbSFA2 by C-terminal tagging with GFP, followed by confocal microscopy. We ﬁrst generated the transgenic parasite lines PbSFA1-GFP and PbSFA2-GFP to localize the proteins individually (Appendix Fig. S3). We were unable to detect GFP signals by live-cell imaging in murine RBCs, likely due to the low expression levels of PbSFAs as evidenced by the need of a high-avidity epitope tag to visualize PfSFAs. Nonetheless, the SFA signals were readily detected during sporozoite formation in oocysts (Fig. 5A,D). Non-synchronized oocysts were imaged at 12–15 days post infection to investigate all steps of sporozoite budding using spinning disc confocal microscopy. Typically, sporozoites are formed over three distinct phases: initiation, intermediate, and elongation. During the initiation phase, the nuclei containing several CPs align below the plasma membrane of the sporoblast, and the IMC is formed beneath the membrane as the membrane generates subtle buds above the nuclei (Araki et al, 2020). The nuclei are oriented with the CP facing the plasma membrane, and the rootlet ﬁber begins to emerge from the CP and connects to the central part of the bud (Schrevel et al, 2008). In the intermediate phase,

the buds begin to elongate and the nuclei separate, with one CP remaining per nucleus, which at this point is still located in the sporoblast cytoplasm. During this phase, a long and electron-dense rootlet ﬁber becomes prominently visible in transmission electron microscopy (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019). Finally, in the elongation phase, each nucleus is packaged into individual elongating buds, followed by a mitochondrion. In oocysts not yet undergoing sporogony, the GFP signal was absent, but during the initiation phase of sporozoite formation, short punctate signals could be detected emanating from the nuclei (Fig. 5A,D ″initiation″ phase). With advancing sporogony, the GFP signals became longer, reaching over 3 μm in length during the elongation phase of sporogony. The Hoechst signals were also elongated at this phase, suggesting that the nuclei were already pulled into the buds (Fig. 5A,D, ″elongation″ phase). On average, the PbSFA1-GFP signal in the elongation phase was 1.6 ± 0.7 μm in length while the PbSFA2-GFP signal was 2.2 ± 0.5 μm in length with aspect ratios of around 5 and 7, respectively (Fig. 5B,E). Once sporozoites were fully formed, the PbSFA1-GFP and PbSFA2-GFP signals disappeared and could not be detected after sporozoite entry into the salivary glands (Fig. 5C,F). These ﬁndings suggest that the two SFAs are part of the rootlet ﬁber that elongates during sporozoite budding and disassembles once sporozoites have formed.

PbSFA KO inhibits sporozoite budding

To investigate the morphological differences of budding sporozoites between the PbSFA-KO mutants and wildtype, we used transmission electron microscopy to analyze chemically ﬁxed and thin-sectioned midguts 12, 15, and 18 days post infection (Fig. 7A,B). Initially, sporozoite buds formed at the plasma membrane in the vicinity of the nuclei (Sterling et al, 1973). In both WT and mutant lines, we found the buds delimited by the inner membrane complex that appeared as a thickened membrane (Fig. 7C,D). In WT parasites, we regularly found a rhoptry anlage in the early buds between the nascent apical end and the nucleus (Fig. 7C). We also found part of the rootlet ﬁber that connected the CP of the nucleus to the nascent apical end (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019) (Fig. 7C). The average length of the rootlet ﬁber was 0.4 ± 0.2 μm at initial budding stage and 1.2 ± 0.4 μm at elongated budding stage, similar to the data from the ﬂuorescence images of the PbSFA1- GFP and PbSFA2-GFP lines. In the mutants, however, rhoptry anlagen were rarely observed and remained in the sporoblast instead of localizing within the budding tip. We also failed to detect any rootlet ﬁber during early budding (Fig. 7D,E). The nuclei, however, were initially positioned below the plasma membrane in mutants just as in wildtype. Intriguingly, some nuclei in the mutants appeared even closer to the nascent apical end, possibly due to the lack of the rhoptry anlage (Fig. 7D). The nucleus is pulled in as sporozoites elongate during budding (Schrevel et al, 2008; Spreng et al, 2019) (Fig. 7C). Yet, in longer protrusions of the mutants we did not ﬁnd any nucleus. Instead, the nuclei of the mutants remained in the sporoblast (Fig. 7F). Also, rhoptries were rarely observed in the elongated buds of mutant parasites and did not appear at the tip of the buds unlike in wildtype. Instead, they often appeared at the rear in conjunction with the mitochondrion or accumulated in the sporoblast (Figs. 7F and EV4B,D). Intriguingly, these rhoptries were electron-dense and elongated, suggesting that they can mature without proper positioning. Mitochondria were found in some elongated buds of the mutants (Figs. 7F and EV4D), which in WT parasites were only packaged into the budding sporozoites once the nucleus was pulled in (Vanderberg and Rhodin 1967). This suggests that mitochondrial packaging might be independent of nuclear packaging, similar to our observations of the PfSFA mutants in the blood stage. The

apicoplast is found near the nucleus in sporozoites (Kudryashev et al, 2010). While we also found apicoplasts in close vicinity of the nuclei inside the buds of budding WT sporozoites (Fig. EV4C), we did not ﬁnd apicoplasts in the buds of mutants. Instead, some apicoplasts were found near nuclei that remained in the sporoblast of the mutants (Fig. EV5E,F), contrary to our observations of the PfSFA mutants in the blood stage. Strikingly, we observed that in parasites lacking either of the PbSFAs, the IMC was not limited to the forming bud but spread across the plasma membrane of the sporoblast, indicating a stark dysfunction in sporozoite formation (Figs. 7F and EV4D,F). The close proximity of mitochondria to the IMC in these mutants might suggest that the transportation and packaging of mitochondria mainly rely on the connection with the IMC, which had also been demonstrated in T. gondii (Oliveira Souza et al, 2022). Together, these data suggest a massive disruption of organelle packaging during sporozoite formation.

3D tomography reveals perturbed inter-organellar relationships in PbSFA mutants

To investigate the previous observations in more detail, we obtained serial sections from chemically ﬁxed infected midguts, generated tomograms from the individual sections, and joined these tomograms into larger volumes (Beyeler et al, 2024; Spreng et al, 2019). In these 3D reconstructions, we could visualize the entire SFA rootlet ﬁber in WT parasites as previously reported (Spreng et al, 2019) (Figs. 8A,B and EV5A–C; Movies EV3 and 4). Interestingly, they also allowed us to visualize an electron-dense spot at the edge of the rhoptry anlagen facing the rootlet ﬁber, indicating a possible connection between the two that may ensure the proper positioning of the rhoptries (Figs. 8A and EV5A and Movie EV3). This density could only be observed in rhoptry anlagen when rootlet ﬁbers were present, suggesting a possible linking function between organelle and ﬁber. Taken together, these 3D data expand on and support the ﬁndings from single sections in mutants lacking either of the PbSFAs, which showed elongated and electron-dense rhoptries in the sporoblast but not in the bud (Figs. 7F and EV4B). We also found elongated rootlet ﬁbers in the WT sporozoites with the nucleus partly pulled into the bud (Figs. 8B and EV5B; Movie EV4). The rootlet ﬁber also appeared in close association with the apicoplast (Fig. EV5B; Movie EV4), but to reveal a possible connection would require further investigation using cryogenic ﬁxation to better preserve the structures. In both elongated sporozoite buds, the mitochondrion was positioned behind the nucleus. The 3D reconstructions of the mutants yielded eight initiating and one elongated budding events for PbSFA1-KO, and seven initiating and two elongated budding events for PbSFA2-KO (Fig. 8C–F; Movies EV5–8). ## Discussion

High-ﬁdelity cell division is a fundamental requirement for all living organisms to ensure accurate transmission of genetic material and proper segregation of cellular components. In model eukaryotes such as yeast and mammalian cells, tightly regulated mitotic checkpoints and cytoskeletal dynamics ensure that chromosomes are duplicated and partitioned evenly, while

organelles are distributed to daughter cells with precision (Gibieža and Petrikaitė, 2021; Jongsma et al, 2015; Kixmoeller et al, 2020; Meraldi et al, 2004). Many fundamental processes required for division are universally conserved, while specialized functions have evolved across different domains of life (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Li, 2013; Sunchu and Cabernard, 2020; Vleugel et al, 2012). The protozoan apicomplexan parasites exhibit highly divergent and often unconventional modes of replication, such as endodyogeny, endopolygeny, schizogony, and binary ﬁssion (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). These modes differ not only in the number of progenies produced per division cycle but also in how nuclei, organelles, and cytoskeletal components are coordinated and partitioned. Despite this diversity, these modes require a high degree of regulation to ensure ﬁdelity, especially given the parasites’ reliance on accurate nuclear and organelle inheritance for infectivity and survival. In Plasmodium, the asexual blood-stage replication cycle and oocyst development represent key points where such ﬁdelity is vital. Using P. falciparum and P. berghei for asexual blood-stage and sexual developmental characterization, respectively, we show here that a rootlet ﬁber made of SFA1 and SFA2 proteins plays a critical role in maintaining this ﬁdelity. An analogous ﬁber in developing Toxoplasma tachyzoites originates from the centrosome, which has long been hypothesized to be an important mediator of all apicomplexan cell division (Francia and Striepen, 2014; Gubbels et al, 2020). The centrosome-equivalent structure in Plasmodium, the CP, functions similarly to other apicomplexan centrosomes, but its unique features, such as a lack of distinct centrioles and other components that make up the T. gondii centrosome, indicate a mechanistic divergence (Mahajan et al, 2008; Tomasina et al, 2021). During replication, the CP is intimately associated with the nucleus and anchors the mitotic spindle, thereby inﬂuencing the accurate segregation of chromosomes. Beyond this function, emerging evidence, including this study, suggests that the cytoplasmic portion of the CP (or the outer-CP) also contributes to the organization and formation of daughter cells through interactions with SFA-based rootlet ﬁbers that extend toward the apical ends of forming daughters (Engelberg et al, 2025; Francia et al, 2012). In schizogony and sporogony, these rootlet ﬁbers form between the CP and the forming apical end, becoming more pronounced during sporogony as they elongate with budding, and disappearing before daughter cell formation is complete. Our observation of anucleate merozoites and sporozoites in SFA-depleted parasites shows that if the outer-CP is no longer connected to the apical end, then the organelles are no longer properly organized in the progeny. In contrast, infectious P. berghei sporozoites failed to form in the absence of either PbSFA1 or PbSFA2 (Fig. 8). Although rare sporozoite-like structures were observed, they lacked nuclei. This difference in nuclear inheritance could have resulted from functional redundancy of nearby structures or components in merozoites. A more likely reason may lie in the intrinsic difference between segmentation during schizogony and budding during sporogony that allows the much smaller merozoites to envelope some of the nuclei by chance due to spatial proximity or crowding, while the nucleus requires tethering to the much longer sporozoite via the rootlet ﬁber to get inside the bud. Thus, the packaging of nuclei into sporozoites may be a more active process than its counterpart in schizogony. We also observed defects in structures associated with the APR, namely the rhoptries and SPMTs. This raises a fundamental question of the apical attachment site of the rootlet ﬁber. While we were unable to discern the exact location of the apical tip of the ﬁber by expansion or electron microscopy, we always localized the tip of the PfSFA2 signal at the space inside the merozoite APR. Similar localization of the rootlet ﬁbers could also be found in sporozoites by electron tomography. Currently, there is little knowledge of the structures in this region besides the apical docking site of the rhoptries (Martinez et al, 2022). The presence of the SFAs near this region suggests that rhoptry biogenesis and proper positioning may be dependent on the rootlet ﬁber or the proximity to the outer-CP. In fact, we observed an electron density potentially linking the rhoptry anlagen in budding sporozoites to the rootlet ﬁber, suggesting that these structures are likely part of a larger complex. Prior studies have demonstrated that rhoptry positioning and maturation are highly ordered processes, thus disruption of the elements coordinating this could contribute to lower merozoite infectivity and failed sporozoite formation (Anaguano et al, 2024; Bannister et al, 2000; Liffner et al, 2021). Intriguingly, rhoptries were rarely found in the elongating sporozoite buds lacking SFAs, but they appeared to be anchored normally, though in varying numbers, in merozoites, suggesting another curious difference between the two stages that awaits molecular explanation. In T. gondii, γ-tubulin, the microtubule nucleation factor, has been localized to the conoid of nascent daughter buds (Engelberg et al, 2025; Haase et al, 2024). However, whether this localization contributes to both intraconoidal MT (ICMT) and SPMT formation, or ICMT alone, is unknown. Since Plasmodium species do not have a distinct conoid-like structure or ICMTs, the nucleation site of cytoplasmic tubulin-based structures, such as the SPMT, remains contested, with the APR and the CP as potential

candidates (Li et al, 2022; Liffner et al, 2023). One to three SPMTs in P. falciparum merozoites and 16 SPMTs in P. berghei sporozoites are attached to the APR. Interestingly, SPMTs are present, albeit perturbed, in SFA-deﬁcient parasites; in reverse, sporozoites lacking SPMTs still show the rootlet ﬁber (Spreng et al, 2019). Indeed, we could observe SPMTs in many anucleate merozoites, although they were fewer in number compared to SPMTs in nucleated merozoites. Similarly, sporozoites in SFA mutants showed fewer microtubules than in wildtype. Because SPMTs are nucleated early in segmentation and budding, the altered positioning and proximity of nuclei to the APRs inside the space-limited parasite could allow for the CP to nucleate and deliver the nascent SPMTs to the APR with a slightly lower efﬁciency. We also found lone microtubules in the sporoblasts of SFA mutants (Fig. EV5D), although nuclei appeared oriented with the CP facing the budding sites as in wildtype. Together, these data suggest that SFAs inﬂuence SPMT formation and/or stability either directly or indirectly, e.g., via their role in maintaining CP connection to the nascent apical ends of daughter cells. However, more work is needed to unambiguously show the origin of SPMT nucleation. Other organelles that require partitioning into merozoites and sporozoites and have previously been linked to the nucleus include the apicoplast and mitochondrion (Kudryashev et al, 2010; Schrevel et al, 2008; Verhoef et al, 2024). However, our data in merozoites show that their inheritance can occur in the absence of a nucleus, implying that their partitioning and/or maintenance mechanisms do not absolutely require a connection to the nucleus/CP. This suggests that the function of the SFA rootlet ﬁber, and to a certain degree the CP, is speciﬁc to nuclear division and structures that require spatial anchoring to the apical complex of the merozoite, such as rhoptries and SPMTs, and are less directly critical for mitochondrial and apicoplast maintenance in the daughter cells. Inside SFA-mutant oocysts, the few anucleate sporozoite-like buds still contained a mitochondrion but lacked the apicoplast, suggesting that these organelles are packaged in different manners and may utilize different inheritance mechanisms compared to the blood stage. The rootlet ﬁber thus emerges as an upstream component necessary to assemble parasites, but other components must also be present to secure full packaging of all organelles into budding sporozoites. How these organelles are trafﬁcked is still unclear. Another curious ﬁnding in oocysts lacking SFAs is a wide spreading of the IMC across the sporoblast membrane in a manner reminiscent of parasites lacking circumsporozoite protein (CSP) (Thathy et al, 2002). The IMC may thus serve as a secondary organizing principle, potentially by binding organelles, as has been previously suggested (Kudryashev et al, 2010). The similarities and differences in phenotype due to the absence of the rootlet ﬁber between merozoites and sporozoites not only expand the role of SFAs and CP in regulating cell division more broadly but also underscore the architectural variations in cell division mechanisms across different life-cycle stages. Further studies are needed to distinguish whether SFAs play an active or passive role during the segmentation or budding of merozoites and sporozoites. Considering the broader parasite life cycle, we also surveyed the sexual developmental stages from gametocytogenesis to ookinete formation in P. berghei. These investigations corroborated our hypothesis that gametocyte formation and sexual commitment would be minimally affected by SFA mutants because nuclear inheritance does not take place. Interestingly, our data suggest a role for SFAs in efﬁcient male gametogenesis, subsequent ookinete conversion, and oocyst formation. These are all stages that require movement of the nucleus within the cell. Alternatively, the SFAs may function in the basal body of the male gamete in a manner similar to Chlamydomonas to contribute to successful and efﬁcient exﬂagellation and zygote formation. Recently, a study identiﬁed a protein, Calcifer, that keeps the basal body physically intact (Guan et al, 2026), and SFAs might play a similar role in basal body anchorage. This could be investigated with V5-tagged SFAs in the future as the GFP-tagged PbSFAs revealed no speciﬁc signal in gametocytes. Ookinetes inside the mosquito midgut undergo extensive cytoskeletal remodeling. Whether SFAs contribute to this process remains to be investigated, but they may be involved in nuclear positioning or apical complex formation, though likely to a lesser degree since oocyst formation is not majorly affected. In addition, the SFA1 mutants in both species of Plasmodium impart slightly more severe phenotypes across different life-cycle stages than their SFA2 counterparts, suggesting that SFA2 may have a stronger compensatory ability to support partial ﬁber formation. Alternatively, SFA1 may play a more important function in ﬁber biogenesis, which is supported by the appearance of the prominent, long, and thick striated structure inside the buds of PbSFA2-KO oocysts (Fig. 8F). Studying asexual replication that occurs inside the vertebrate liver would likely produce compelling companion data for our blood-stage ﬁndings. However, because SFAs are essential for sporozoite formation, stage-speciﬁc inducible KO or expression of SFAs under a sporogenesis-speciﬁc promoter would be required to interrogate their function during the liver stage. Since parasites undergo a similar albeit distinct process of schizogony in the liver compared to the intraerythrocytic version, we hypothesize that SFAs are also important during this stage (Roques et al, 2023). Overall, the SFA function linking the CP and forming daughter cells presented in this study is likely conserved across Plasmodium species and across replicative stages inside the vertebrate liver, RBCs, and mosquito midgut. A recent study in T. gondii has revealed novel proteins colocalizing with the SFA rootlet ﬁber: TgSFA4 (TGGT1_293170/ PF3D7_1447800), TgSFA5 (TGGT1_212780), and TGGT1_246740/PF3D7_1346000 (Li et al, 2024b). TgSFA5 was found to be essential for daughter cell formation, but it is a Sarcocystidae-speciﬁc protein. TgSFA4 and TGGT1_246740 both

have homologs in Plasmodium. We also investigated interactors of the SFA rootlet ﬁber in P. falciparum schizonts using PfSFA2 as a co-IP bait. The TgSFA4 ortholog was identiﬁed in our co-IP data but predicted to be dispensable (Dataset EV1) (Zhang et al, 2018). Beyond PfSFA1, which appeared as a top hit, this study also focused on two putative interactors of PfSFA2 – PF3D7_0703600 and PfPEARL. Both localized closely with PfSFA2 in schizonts— PF3D7_0703600 localized toward the basal end of the rootlet ﬁber, while PfPEARL localized toward the apical end. PF3D7_0703600 is a β-giardin-like protein with a similar protein size and predicted α- helical structure to alveolate SFAs. β-giardins belong to the larger SFA family proteins and have been shown to localize to the microtubule-associated Giardia ventral disc (Heiss et al, 2025; Nosala et al, 2020; Palm et al, 2005). Its role outside of Giardia is unknown, but our study presents initial evidence that PF3D7_0703600 may serve as an accessory protein to the SFA ﬁber, potentially as a linker between PfSFA2 and the outer-CP. Albeit limited, the evidence for this hypothesized function comes from the immunoﬂuorescence signal of PF3D7_0703600 overlapping with the outer-CP end of PfSFA2 and extending toward the nucleus. Its ortholog in P. berghei, PBANKA_0801300, may localize similarly, but detailed functional characterization in both species is needed to determine their speciﬁc role during schizogony and their relation to the SFA rootlet ﬁber. PfPEARL, on the other hand, seems to only be present in some primate Plasmodium species, and no obvious ortholog exists in P. berghei (Aurrecoechea et al, 2009). This protein partially colocalized with PfSFA2 during nascent apical pole generation and localized at the junction between the elongated SFA rootlet ﬁber and APR by the onset of segmentation. PfPEARL-KD had similar growth and morphological defects as PfSFA-KO—partial disconnection between the nuclei and forming merozoites, as well as dysregulated rhoptry formation. Rhoptries also seemed to aggregate in the residual body more often than in PfSFA-KO parasites. Strikingly, simultaneous depletion of PfPEARL and PfSFA2 led to a more severe segmentation defect and a complete arrest of bloodstage replication. Based on these ﬁndings, we hypothesize that PfPEARL is an accessory component of the SFA rootlet ﬁber and/or a linker between the ﬁber and the apical pole of forming daughter cells. In the absence of PfSFAs, PfPEARL may be able to partially maintain the connection between some of the nucleus-daughter cell pairs, and vice versa. PfPEARL may also occupy a distinct region between the rootlet ﬁber and the apical pole, as evidenced by its more apical localization prior to segmentation. This leads us to hypothesize that it may also play a more direct role in regulating rhoptry biogenesis, further supported by PfPEARL-deﬁcient schizonts exhibiting more severe dysregulation of rhoptry formation than PfSFA-deﬁcient parasites. An orthologous region contributing to APR-rootlet connection may also exist in P. berghei, but the lack of PfPEARL in the genome suggests that there are differences in the composition of SFA accessory proteins between these species. Other accessory proteins serving PfPEARLlike function may also exist, since the KD of PfPEARL alone did not completely ablate the formation of the SFA ﬁber between the outer- CP and APR (Fig. EV3). Therefore, studying other uncharacterized proteins pulled down with PfSFA2 (Dataset EV1) is necessary to resolve this apical connection more completely and further delineate the function of SFAs at the apical tip of the forming daughter cells.

Finally, the absence of SFAs in vertebrates and their divergent and central function across several life-cycle stages of Plasmodium position them as bona ﬁde targets for antimalarial intervention. Compounds that destabilize SFA ﬁbers or interfere with their interaction with the CP would disrupt parasite development at multiple bottlenecks, including blood-stage replication and sporozoite formation. Overall, we have demonstrated a signiﬁcant role that SFAs play in daughter cell formation across the Plasmodium life cycle. The use of P. falciparum and P. berghei allowed us to leverage the complementary strengths of each system: high-resolution characterization of SFA localization and function during human blood-stage replication in P. falciparum, and genetic interrogation of SFA function during experimentally tractable mosquito-stage development in P. berghei. Although this division necessarily limits direct comparisons across life-cycle stages and species, the concordance of SFA localization and perturbation phenotypes supports a conserved role for the SFA rootlet ﬁber during replicative stages. By connecting the CP with the apical pole of forming daughter cells, the SFA rootlet ﬁber ensures that each daughter cell faithfully receives one copy of the nucleus, and that its apical complex properly forms. Future work should focus on delineating the complete molecular composition of SFA rootlet ﬁber and CP, as well as the signaling pathways that regulate their dynamics.

Phylogenetic tree

A maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree of eight SFA orthologs in Plasmodium falciparum, P. berghei, Toxoplasma gondii, and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii were constructed in MEGA X using the JTT substitution model. Electron microscopy

To prepare samples for transmission electron microscopy, infected midguts from female mosquitoes were dissected at 12-, 15-, and 18- days post infection, and those midguts selected showed a high infection. The whole ﬁxation and embedding process was performed in the microwave (BioWave Pro+, Ted Pella Inc, Redding, CA, USA), and samples were cooled on ice when being microwaved. Midguts were chemically ﬁxed in 4% PFA & 1% glutaraldehyde in 100 mM PHEM buffer (60 mM PIPES, 25 mM HEPES, 10 mM EGTA, and 2 mM MgSO4) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 Watts power for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min, so in total 14 min). Samples were washed twice in 100 mM PHEM buffer by microwaving samples at 250 W for 1 min. A secondary ﬁxation was done in 1% osmium tetroxide (in 100 mM PHEM buffer) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 W for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min). Osmium tetroxide was removed by washing the sample twice in distilled water at 250 W for 1 min. Samples were then contrasted with 1% uranyl acetate (in ddH2O) for 8 min (with 2 min break every 2 min) at 20 Hg vacuum and 100 Watts. Samples were washed twice with distilled water as before and dehydrated for 40 s at 250 Watts in increasing concentrations of aqueous acetone (30%, 50, 70, and 90) and twice in 100% dried acetone. Samples were transferred to Spurr’s solution [23.6% epoxycyclohexyl- methyl- 3,4- epoxycyclohexylcarboxylate (ERL), 14.2% ERL- 4206 plasticizer, 61.3% nonenylsuccinic anhydride, 0.9% dimethylethanolamine] by being immersed in increasing concentrations of Spurr resin (25, 50, 75% in acetone) for 3 min each at 20 Hg vacuum and 250 W and ﬁnally immersed in 100% Spurr resin for 3 min at 20 Hg vacuum and 250 W. Samples were then immersed in 100% Spurr resin at room temperature overnight and polymerized afterward at 60 °C for at least 48 h. Embedded midguts were sectioned using an ultramicrotome (LEICA EM UC7, Leica Microsystems GmbH). About 1-μm-thick sections were collected for toluidine blue staining to check for oocysts in the current cutting plane. About 80- to 100-nm-thick single sections were acquired for 2D imaging, and 200-nm-thick serial sections were acquired for electron tomography. Sections were imaged on a transmission electron microscope at 200 kV (FEI Tecnai F20, FEI, Eindhoven, Netherlands) using an Eagle 4k × 4k CCD camera (FEI Eindhoven, Netherlands) using SerialEM version 4.1.18(Mastronarde, 2005).

Electron tomography

For tomography, bidirectional single-axis tilt series were taken from −60° to +60° with 2° increments. Tilt series of WT, SFA1KO and SFA2KO budding initiation, and WT and SFA1KO budding elongation were taken at 11,500X magniﬁcation resulting in a pixel size of 0.953 nm. A tilt series of SFA2KO budding elongation were taken at 9600X, resulting in a pixel size of 1.12 nm. Tilt series

were reconstructed into tomograms and joined into larger volumes using IMOD (Kremer et al, 1996). Eventually, three volumes were joined to a thickness of about 800 nm for budding initiations and three volumes of about 1.5 μm for budding elongations. Since this does not account for beam-induced shrinkage, the original depth covered may be greater. Segmentation of the cellular structures and visualization in 3D were performed using IMOD after isotropic binning by a factor of 2 to reduce ﬁle size.
